t: Minimum Operations to Make the Array Increasing — Greedy Prefix Sweep
o:
**Understanding the problem**

Each operation increments one element by 1, and we want the fewest operations so that nums becomes strictly increasing (nums[i] < nums[i+1]). Example 1 ([1,1,1]): raise element 1 to 2 and element 2 to 3 — three operations total. Example 2 ([1,5,2,4,1]): fix the tail to 6, 7, 8, costing 4 + 3 + 7 = 14. Example 3 ([8]) needs nothing. Constraints are tiny (n <= 5000, values <= 10^4), so any polynomial method passes — but only increments exist, which pins down the optimal move: every violation must be repaired by lifting the current element to exactly previous + 1, since anything lower keeps the violation and anything higher wastes moves.
k: With increments-only, the cheapest legal value for a violating element is exactly previous + 1, never more.
Fixing each element minimally also minimizes the requirement imposed on the next element — an exchange argument proves greedy optimality.
A single pass suffices, O(1) extra space; the answer (at most about 5000 * 10^4) fits in a 32-bit integer.

a.i: Copy the array and walk it, mutating exactly as described: whenever arr[i] <= arr[i-1], raise arr[i] to arr[i-1] + 1 and bank the number of unit steps spent. This simulation makes the greedy concrete and trivially verifiable.
s: Copy nums into arr; initialize ops = 0.
For i from 1 to n-1: if arr[i] <= arr[i-1], add arr[i-1] + 1 - arr[i] to both ops and arr[i].
a.t: O(n) — a single pass over the array

a.n: Approach 2: Track the Previous Effective Value
a.i: No mutation is needed: keep prev, the value the previous element was raised to. If the current x already exceeds prev, carry it forward untouched; otherwise pay prev + 1 - x operations and set prev to prev + 1 (the raised value of x). Identical decisions to the simulation without the auxiliary array.
s: For each x: if x <= prev, add prev + 1 - x to ops and increment prev by 1; otherwise set prev = x.

w:
**Wrap-up**

Present the copy-based simulation first, then note the O(1)-space refinement — interviewers appreciate seeing the reduction immediately. Pitfalls: using >= instead of > (the target is STRICTLY increasing), forgetting that subsequent elements compare against the RAISED value rather than the original, and decrementing elements (not permitted). Single-element arrays need zero operations. Follow-up: if decrements were also allowed, the same sweep applies per pair using absolute differences; if you could set any value in one operation, each violation would cost exactly 1.
